latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Quantitative load of S. pneumoniae replicating in distal airways and alveoli. The proximate driver of all downstream pathology; declines with adequate antibiotic coverage and rises with resistance or delayed therapy.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Capsular polysaccharide-mediated complement and opsonin evasion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Polysaccharide capsule prevents C3b deposition and phagocytosis, the dominant virulence factor that allows replication in immunocompetent hosts and is the basis for serotype-specific outcome differences (e.g., serotype 3 thick capsule, more necrotizing/invasive disease).

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pneumolysin-mediated alveolar epithelial and endothelial injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cholesterol-dependent pore-forming cytolysin disrupts alveolar epithelial-endothelial barrier, drives protein-rich exudate (the 'red and gray hepatization' substrate), activates complement, and contributes to capillary leak and consolidation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Neutrophilic alveolar exudation and lobar consolidation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Massive neutrophil influx, fibrin and red cell extravasation filling alveoli, producing the classic lobar consolidation that is radiographically dense and air-bronchograms positive. Drives shunt physiology and hypoxemia.
Innate immune cytokine cascade driving fever, rigors, tachycardia, CRP and procalcitonin elevation, hyponatremia (SIADH), and ferritin rise. Magnitude predicts severity and shock risk.

Hematogenous spread from alveolar focus, present in ~20-30% of hospitalized pneumococcal pneumonia. Gateway to metastatic disease (meningitis, endocarditis, septic arthritis) and a key driver of distributive shock and mortality.

Visceral pleural inflammation adjacent to consolidation produces pleuritic chest pain and exudative effusion. Sterile early; can transition to complicated effusion (low pH, low glucose, high LDH) and frank empyema if not drained.

Bacterial invasion of pleural space with frank pus and loculation; requires source control (chest tube ± fibrinolytics ± VATS). Persistent fever and inflammatory markers despite appropriate antibiotics is the cardinal warning sign.

Tissue destruction with cavitation, classically associated with serotype 3 and other thick-capsule serotypes. Predicts prolonged course, higher mortality, and need for prolonged antibiotics; rarely surgical resection.
Cytokine-mediated vasoplegia with hypotension, lactate rise, AKI, SOFA elevation; the dominant mortality pathway in severe pneumococcal pneumonia, especially with bacteremia or asplenia.

CNS seeding from bacteremia, particularly in asplenia, CSF leak, cochlear implants. Manifests as fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status; demands urgent CSF sampling and high-dose ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pneumococcal endocarditis (Austrian syndrome when with meningitis)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Rare but devastating valve seeding from bacteremia, classically aortic, often with valve destruction and high mortality. Triad of pneumonia + meningitis + endocarditis = Austrian syndrome.

In asplenic or hyposplenic hosts, absence of splenic IgM-memory B cells and macrophage filtration allows uncontrolled bacteremia, DIC, purpura fulminans, Waterhouse-Friderichsen-like adrenal hemorrhage, and mortality within hours despite ICU care. Distinct biology from non-asplenic shock.

Penicillin-binding protein 1a/2b/2x mosaic gene alterations elevate penicillin and ceftriaxone MIC. For non-meningeal pneumonia, intermediate resistance often surmountable with high-dose β-lactam; for meningitis, vancomycin + ceftriaxone required.

Ribosomal methylation (ermB) or efflux (mefA) drives macrolide resistance; prevalence regionally high (>30% in many areas including East Asia and US). Macrolide monotherapy fails when resistance present; combination β-lactam + macrolide partially mitigates via immunomodulation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Post-influenza alveolar epithelial denudation enabling pneumococcal superinfection
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Influenza-mediated ciliated epithelial damage, exposed lung-receptor binding sites, and type I IFN-induced suppression of alveolar macrophage antibacterial function create a 1-2 week window of dramatically increased pneumococcal pneumonia risk and severity.
Consolidated lung produces V/Q mismatch dominated by true shunt; refractory hypoxemia, increasing FiO2 requirement, and progression to ARDS-physiology when bilateral and severe.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Capsule prevents opsonophagocytosis, permitting unchecked alveolar replication; serotype-specific capsule thickness explains burden differences.
Pneumolysin release scales with bacterial load; greater burden produces more pore-forming toxin and barrier disruption.
Pneumolysin and bacterial PAMPs (PGN, lipoteichoic acid) recruit neutrophils via complement and chemokine activation, producing exudative consolidation.
Alveolar exudate fills airspaces lobe-by-lobe producing dense radiographic consolidation with air bronchograms.
Generic infiltrate extent rises with neutrophilic exudate volume; multilobar involvement raises severity.
Consolidated alveoli produce true shunt physiology and FiO2-refractory hypoxemia.
Shunt physiology drops SpO2 disproportionately to FiO2 increase.
P/F ratio is the canonical severity marker; <300 mild ARDS, <200 moderate, <100 severe.
Tachypnea is the earliest and most sensitive vital sign change in pneumonia and a CURB-65 component.
Bilateral or multilobar pneumococcal pneumonia is a leading non-ARDS-prototype cause of ARDS.
Severe hypoxemia or work of breathing failure mandates intubation; HFNC/NIV may bridge in selected cases.
Productive cough with characteristically rust-colored sputum from RBC extravasation through injured alveolar capillaries.
Classic rusty sputum reflects red-cell extravasation in the red hepatization phase; not pathognomonic but highly suggestive.
Loss of functional alveolar units and increased work of breathing produce dyspnea proportional to extent.
Consolidated lung transmits central airway sounds: bronchial breath sounds, increased tactile fremitus, egophony, whispered pectoriloquy.
Air-replaced-by-fluid territory percusses dull; complemented by stony dullness if effusion present.
Inspiratory crackles from opening of fluid-filled alveoli; persist into recovery as resolution proceeds.
Pleural surface inflammation produces sharp, breathing-related pain that often dominates the presentation.
Up to 40% of hospitalized pneumococcal pneumonia develop a parapneumonic effusion; majority sterile and self-resolving with antibiotics.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: delayed or inadequate antibiotic therapy and absence of drainage
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Untreated complicated effusion (low pH, low glucose, high LDH, positive Gram stain or culture) progresses to frank empyema.
Imaging or thoracentesis confirms loculated pus; CT defines loculation pattern guiding chest tube vs VATS.
Conversion to frank empyema mandates source control and prolongs antibiotic course to 4-6 weeks.
Empyema is a source-control problem; antibiotics alone fail without drainage.
Alveolar replication breaches capillary barrier producing bacteremia in 20-30% of hospitalized cases.
Yield collapses rapidly after first antibiotic dose; pre-antibiotic cultures essential.
Bacteremia amplifies systemic cytokine signal and is an independent predictor of shock and mortality.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: CSF leak, cochlear implant, asplenia, or hematogenous seeding
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Pneumococcus is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults; pneumonia + meningitis classic combination.
Rare but classic Austrian syndrome (pneumonia + meningitis + endocarditis), often aortic valve, with destructive course.
Bacteremia in pneumococcal pneumonia confers measurable meningitis hazard, especially in vulnerable hosts.
Altered mental status in pneumococcal pneumonia mandates LP to exclude meningitis (also a CURB-65 marker).
New murmur, persistent bacteremia, or embolic phenomena should prompt TTE/TEE.
Bacterial PAMPs activate TLR/NLR signaling driving IL-6/TNF/IL-1β.
Endogenous pyrogen-driven fever, often abrupt with rigors at onset; defervescence by day 3-5 is the canonical antibiotic response signal.
Single dramatic rigor at onset is classic for pneumococcal pneumonia; suggests bacteremic disease.
Cytokine and fever-driven sinus tachycardia; persistent tachycardia despite defervescence suggests complication.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute phase; CRP typically >100 mg/L in pneumococcal pneumonia, trajectory tracks treatment response.
PCT rises faster than CRP and more specific for bacterial infection; useful for guiding antibiotic duration.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis typical; leukopenia <4 (paradoxical) is a CURB-65/severity marker indicating poor response.
Left shift with bands and toxic granulation reflects marrow demand from bacterial infection.
Neutrophilia drives the WBC rise; severe sepsis may produce neutropenia in marrow exhaustion.
SIADH from cytokine-driven non-osmotic ADH release; hyponatremia common in pneumococcal pneumonia and Legionella.
Patient-reported fever onset is acute and dramatic in classic pneumococcal pneumonia.
Vasoplegia drops MAP; <65 mmHg is qSOFA criterion and vasopressor threshold.
SBP <90 is a CURB-65 component; widened pulse pressure with low DBP characterizes early distributive shock.
Tissue hypoperfusion and adrenergic stress drive lactate; >2 mmol/L sepsis criterion, >4 mmol/L severe.
Multiorgan dysfunction integrates all shock-related deteriorations; ΔSOFA ≥2 defines sepsis.
Hypoperfusion ATN is the dominant AKI mechanism; recovery typical with shock reversal.
Vasopressor requirement plus lactate >2 defines septic shock by Sepsis-3.
Oliguria is an early hypoperfusion signal preceding creatinine rise.
AKI develops over 1-3 days from shock-induced ATN.
BUN >19 mg/dL (>7 mmol/L) is the CURB-65 'U' component capturing prerenal/AKI severity.
Lactic acidosis lowers bicarbonate; widening anion gap.
Sepsis-associated thrombocytopenia and DIC consumption; thrombocytopenia is a SOFA component and severity marker.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: asplenia, hyposplenia, or sickle cell disease
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mortality of OPSI 50-70% even with prompt ICU care; demands immediate empiric ceftriaxone at first fever and lifelong vaccination.
OPSI accelerates the shock pathway dramatically; death within 24-48 hours of presentation typical.
Cavitation on CT, especially in serotype 3 or among children, indicates necrotizing pneumonia and prolonged course.
Necrotizing transformation is associated with longer fever duration, higher mortality, and need for prolonged antibiotic therapy.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: if empiric coverage relies on β-lactam at standard dose
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Elevated MIC reduces probability of coverage at standard dosing; high-dose β-lactam often retains activity for non-meningeal disease.
PBP2x mutations elevate ceftriaxone MIC; susceptibility breakpoints differ for meningeal vs non-meningeal sites.
Macrolide monotherapy fails in resistant strains; combination β-lactam + macrolide is preferred for severe CAP partly due to macrolide immunomodulation.
Post-influenza superinfection is the deadliest pneumococcal pneumonia phenotype historically; biphasic illness with worsening after initial influenza improvement is the pattern to recognize.
BinaxNOW-type C-polysaccharide antigen detection has ~70% sensitivity in adults, higher in bacteremic disease; remains positive for days even after antibiotics.
Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci on a quality sputum specimen, especially with abundant PMNs, supports pneumococcal etiology.
Culture provides species confirmation and susceptibility but is yield-limited (~30-50%) and rapidly lost after antibiotics.
Combined urinary antigen + Gram stain + culture + blood cultures together raise diagnostic confidence; etiologic confirmation remains <50% in CAP overall.
Septic shock is the dominant proximate cause of death in pneumococcal pneumonia (mortality 20-50% in severe CAP with shock).
ARDS-physiology pneumococcal pneumonia carries high mortality even with lung-protective ventilation.
OPSI mortality 50-70% within 24-48 hours; the most acute mortality pathway in this disease.
Pneumococcal meningitis mortality 15-25% with appropriate therapy; pneumonia + meningitis dual pathology compounds risk.
Necrotizing transformation prolongs course and elevates mortality, especially in elderly and comorbid hosts.
Mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, and broad-spectrum antibiotics raise risk of nosocomial superinfection (VAP, C. difficile, line infection).
HSV-1 reactivation during pneumococcal pneumonia is a classic clinical sign reflecting acute illness stress; not causal but disease-supportive.
Multilobar involvement marks more severe disease and predicts ICU admission and ARDS.
Added during horizontal ontology audit: this axis is a real shared inflammatory/CNS involvement feature for this disease family, not a case-specific ranking patch.
Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing oxygen_saturation pathway.

axes.shape_free_text: Abrupt rise to 39-40°C with rigors at onset; defervescence by day 3-5 with appropriate antibiotics; persistent fever beyond day 5 suggests empyema, resistance, metastatic focus, or necrotizing transformation.
Sinus tachycardia from fever and cytokines; persistent tachycardia >100 despite defervescence raises concern for empyema, PE, or shock.
Tachypnea is the earliest and most sensitive vital sign; ≥30 is a CURB-65 component.
Stable in uncomplicated; falls in shock; SBP <90 is CURB-65 component.
MAP <65 indicates shock requiring vasopressors.
Falls with extent of consolidation; resistant to FiO2 increase due to shunt.

Oxygen or ventilatory support requirement: 0 room air, 1 low-flow nasal cannula, 2 mask or higher low-flow support, 3 high-flow nasal cannula, 4 noninvasive ventilation, 5 invasive ventilation or extracorporeal support.
Drops with severity; <300 mild ARDS, <200 moderate, <100 severe.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis 15-30; leukopenia <4 is paradoxical and severity marker.
Drives WBC rise; consumed in severe sepsis with marrow exhaustion.
Left shift with bands and toxic granulation.
Typically >100 mg/L, often >200; trajectory tracks treatment response with half-life ~2 days.
Rises rapidly, useful for distinguishing bacterial CAP and guiding antibiotic discontinuation.
Rises in shock; >2 sepsis, >4 severe.
Rises with prerenal/AKI in shock; recovers with resuscitation.
BUN >19 (>7 mmol/L) is the CURB-65 'U' component.
Hyponatremia common from SIADH; severe (<130) more typical of Legionella but seen in pneumococcal.
Falls with lactic acidosis in shock.
May rise reactively or fall in sepsis/DIC; thrombocytopenia is severity marker.
Stable typically; falls if anemia of inflammation prolonged.
Falls with capillary leak and acute phase suppression.
Mild rise with sepsis/hepatic perfusion compromise; marked rise in DIC.
Composite organ dysfunction; ΔSOFA ≥2 defines sepsis.
Confusion / Urea>7 / RR≥30 / BP<90 or DBP≤60 / Age≥65; 0-1 outpatient, 2 admit, ≥3 ICU consideration.
Pneumonia Severity Index, more granular than CURB-65; class IV-V predict high mortality.
Drops in shock and AKI; <0.5 mL/kg/hr concerning.
Confusion is a CURB-65 component; new altered mental status mandates LP to exclude meningitis.
Productive cough; classically with rust-colored sputum.
Pathognomonic-suggestive finding from RBC extravasation in red hepatization phase; not always present but highly specific.
Proportional to extent and oxygenation impairment.
Pleuritic chest pain from parapneumonic pleuritis is a hallmark feature.
Single dramatic shaking chill at onset; predicts bacteremic disease.
Acute high-grade fever onset; key history element.
Tubular bronchial breathing over consolidation; with egophony, increased fremitus, whispered pectoriloquy.
Dull over consolidation; stony dull suggests effusion.
Inspiratory crackles common; persist into resolution.
Classic finding of HSV-1 reactivation during pneumococcal pneumonia.
Generic infiltrate burden; rises with consolidation.
Dense lobar consolidation with air bronchograms is the canonical imaging pattern; resolution lags clinical recovery 2-8 weeks.
Multilobar disease is a severity criterion (ATS/IDSA minor criterion) and predicts ICU need.
Up to 40% of hospitalized cases; mostly small and self-resolving.
Loculated pus on imaging or pleural pH<7.2/glucose<40/positive culture; mandates drainage.
Cavitation indicates necrotizing pneumonia (often serotype 3); prolonged course.
C-polysaccharide antigen detection ~70% sensitivity in adults, higher with bacteremia; remains positive days into therapy; not for children due to false positives.
Positive in 20-30% of hospitalized; highest yield if drawn pre-antibiotic.
Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci in pairs/short chains with PMNs; quality-dependent.
Yield 30-50% pre-antibiotic, much lower after; provides susceptibility.
Serotype 3 (thick mucoid capsule) associated with necrotizing disease, empyema, higher mortality, and reduced PCV13 effectiveness.
MIC <2 non-meningeal susceptible at high dose; ≥4 resistant. Meningeal breakpoints stricter.
Most pneumococcal isolates susceptible to ceftriaxone at non-meningeal breakpoints.
Drug-resistant S. pneumoniae risk factors: age >65, β-lactam in past 3-6 months, alcoholism, multiple comorbidities, immunosuppression, daycare exposure.
Regionally high (>30% in much of US, Asia); macrolide monotherapy not recommended in regions with >25% resistance.
True IgE-mediated penicillin allergy <5% of self-reported; skin testing useful.
0=unvaccinated, 1=PPSV23 only, 2=PCV13/15/20 only, 3=combined sequential schedule per ACIP.
Anatomic asplenia (post-splenectomy), functional asplenia (sickle cell, advanced cirrhosis, celiac), or hyposplenia. Massive risk amplifier for OPSI.
Window of 1-2 weeks after acute influenza when pneumococcal superinfection risk is highest; biphasic illness pattern.
Probability that empiric regimen covers the actual organism at adequate exposure.
Clinical instability, persistent fever, or worsening at 72h after empiric therapy; triggers re-evaluation for empyema, resistance, alternate diagnosis.
Pulmonary source ~1.0 by definition; relevant for shock workup.
Rises when complicated effusion or empyema present.
Adequate when chest tube/VATS achieves drainage; inadequate predicts ongoing fever.
Volume drained, lung re-expansion, defervescence after tube placement; loculation requires fibrinolytics or VATS.
Combined microbiologic confidence; <0.5 in roughly half of CAP cases despite full workup.
HIV, chemotherapy, biologics, chronic steroid use; broadens differential and raises severity.
Highest risk in multilobar pneumococcal pneumonia with shock; ~10-15% of severe CAP develop ARDS.
Increases with severity and FiO2 requirement.
AKI hazard tracks shock and nephrotoxin exposure.
Hazard rises with bacteremia, multilobar disease, asplenia, age.
ICU-acquired infections: VAP, CRBSI, C. difficile.
Risk peaks days 4-14 if effusion present without drainage.
Highest with bacteremia, asplenia, CSF leak, cochlear implant.
Rare but devastating; consider with persistent bacteremia, new murmur.
Higher with serotype 3 and pediatric/immunocompromised hosts.
Massive elevation in asplenic hosts with rapid trajectory to DIC and death.
Aggregate disease-specific mortality. Outpatient CAP <1%; hospitalized 5-15%; ICU 20-50%; OPSI 50-70%; bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia 10-20% even with treatment.
Nonspecific systemic inflammatory marker that commonly rises in clinically significant pulmonary, metastatic, or disseminated infection; included through horizontal fairness audit.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both driven by IL-6 acute phase response; PCT rises and falls faster than CRP creating a small lead-lag pattern.
Each 1°C rise typically adds 8-10 bpm; persistent tachycardia after defervescence flags complication.
Tachypnea compensates for hypoxemia; both worsen together as consolidation extends.
Larger and more persistent effusions are at highest risk for transition to empyema if not drained.
Bacteremia is an independent predictor of progression to shock and mortality.
Anatomic/functional asplenia is the dominant risk factor for OPSI; mortality dramatically elevated.
Vaccination reduces invasive disease incidence and severity; doesn't fully eliminate risk especially serotypes outside vaccine.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: MIC ≥4 μg/mL non-meningeal resistant; high-dose penicillin/ampicillin can overcome intermediate (MIC 2-4) for non-meningeal disease.
True IgE-mediated penicillin allergy precludes use; cross-reactivity with cephalosporins now estimated <2%.
CSF penetration limited; meningitis suspicion shifts to ceftriaxone + vancomycin.

side_effects.interpretation: C. difficile and yeast superinfection risk modest with narrow-spectrum penicillin.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive narrow-spectrum therapy when susceptibility confirmed; preferred de-escalation target.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Reduced susceptibility lowers empiric coverage probability.
Ceftriaxone achieves bactericidal CSF concentrations; backbone for pneumococcal meningitis (combined with vancomycin and dexamethasone).
History of anaphylaxis to a β-lactam contraindicates without allergy work-up.

side_effects.interpretation: C. difficile risk modestly elevated with broad-spectrum cephalosporins.

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line empiric IV β-lactam for hospitalized CAP; once-daily dosing convenient.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ermB-mediated high-level resistance produces clinical failure; macrolide monotherapy not recommended where regional resistance >25%.
Macrolide-induced QT prolongation; caution with concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.

side_effects.interpretation: Class effect; matters in patients on multiple QT-prolonging agents or with electrolyte derangements.

treatments.context_specific_role: Combined with β-lactam for severe CAP both for atypical coverage and immunomodulatory benefit; monotherapy only in low-resistance regions and outpatient setting.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Levofloxacin requires renal dose adjustment; moxifloxacin does not.

side_effects.interpretation: Particularly with moxifloxacin and concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.

treatments.context_specific_role: Monotherapy alternative covering pneumococcus + atypicals; useful with β-lactam allergy; reserve to avoid masking TB.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Combined with ceftriaxone + dexamethasone for empiric pneumococcal meningitis until ceftriaxone MIC known.

side_effects.interpretation: Trough-dependent nephrotoxicity, especially with concomitant nephrotoxins.

treatments.context_specific_role: Add for suspected meningitis or highly resistant strains pending susceptibility; not routine for pneumonia alone.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active against highly resistant pneumococcal strains and MRSA when superinfection suspected.

side_effects.interpretation: Thrombocytopenia with use >10-14 days; monitor weekly.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative for highly resistant pneumococcus and MRSA superinfection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibiotics alone fail in frank empyema; drainage is mandatory.

side_effects.interpretation: Modest bleeding risk; corrected coagulopathy first.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source control mandatory for complicated effusion (pH<7.2, glucose<40, positive culture/Gram stain) or frank empyema; intrapleural tPA + DNase for loculated empyema; VATS if failed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe CAP with shock or high inflammatory burden may benefit from short-course steroids (CAPE-COD trial demonstrated mortality benefit with hydrocortisone in severe CAP).
Caution with concurrent influenza coinfection (steroids worsen influenza outcomes); rule out before initiating.

side_effects.interpretation: Modestly elevated nosocomial and opportunistic infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive in severe CAP with shock or high inflammation; not routine in mild-moderate disease; avoid if influenza coinfection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dexamethasone given before or with first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and neurologic sequelae specifically in pneumococcal meningitis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct only when meningitis suspected/confirmed; must be given with or before first antibiotic dose to be effective.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Asplenic patients require both PCV and PPSV23 plus revaccination; antibody response may be blunted.
Reduced antibody response in profound immunosuppression; still recommended.

treatments.context_specific_role: Primary prevention; deploy after recovery in unvaccinated hospitalized pneumococcal pneumonia patients before discharge per ACIP.
Broader serotype coverage than PCV13/15; sequential schedule with PCV per ACIP. PCV20 may obviate PPSV23 in many adults.

over_65.trajectory_modulation: higher mortality, more multilobar disease, atypical presentations (afebrile, confusion-only)

present.trajectory_modulation: OPSI risk; 50-70% mortality if fulminant; mandates immediate empiric ceftriaxone at first fever, lifelong vaccination, antibiotic stand-by

current.trajectory_modulation: impaired mucociliary clearance, more severe disease

present.trajectory_modulation: aspiration risk, impaired neutrophil function, higher mortality, more bacteremia
AECOPD overlap; longer recovery; higher exacerbation hazard

hiv_positive_cd4_under_200.trajectory_modulation: much higher bacteremia rate, recurrent disease, broader differential including PCP

present.trajectory_modulation: blunted febrile response, atypical presentation, higher mortality
acute decompensation risk; volume management complexity
functional hyposplenism, complement deficiency, much higher mortality

within_2_weeks.trajectory_modulation: post-influenza pneumococcal superinfection is the deadliest CAP phenotype historically

present.trajectory_modulation: functional asplenia; pediatric prophylactic penicillin standard until age 5
elevated meningitis hazard; aggressive vaccination required

pcv13_or_higher.trajectory_modulation: lower invasive disease incidence and mortality; serotype-replacement disease may persist

present.trajectory_modulation: higher resistance prevalence; broader empiric coverage often warranted
elevates DRSP probability; shifts empiric choice

supportive_care: oxygen supplementation titrated to SpO2 92-96% (88-92% in chronic hypercapnia)
non-invasive ventilation or HFNC for selected patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure
early invasive mechanical ventilation with lung-protective settings (Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau <30) when ARDS develops
IV crystalloid resuscitation at 30 mL/kg in sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, then individualized
norepinephrine first-line vasopressor for septic shock targeting MAP ≥65
add vasopressin and/or epinephrine as second-line vasopressors

obtain blood cultures × 2 sets, sputum Gram stain and culture, urinary pneumococcal antigen, urinary Legionella antigen, and respiratory viral PCR including influenza and SARS-CoV-2 before first antibiotic dose when feasible
chest imaging (CXR PA + lateral, escalate to CT if suspicion of empyema, abscess, cavitation, or non-resolving pneumonia)
timely first antibiotic dose (within 1 hour of sepsis recognition, within 4 hours of CAP diagnosis)
de-escalation to narrow-spectrum agent guided by culture and susceptibility once stable
oral switch when clinically stable (afebrile 24h, hemodynamically stable, tolerating PO, improving oxygenation)
total antibiotic duration typically 5-7 days for uncomplicated CAP, 7-10 days for bacteremic, 2-3 weeks for empyema, 4-6 weeks for complicated empyema or metastatic infection
thoracentesis with pleural fluid pH, glucose, LDH, protein, cell count, Gram stain, and culture for any effusion >10 mm on lateral decubitus
chest tube drainage for complicated parapneumonic effusion (pH<7.2, glucose<40 mg/dL, positive Gram stain or culture) or frank empyema
intrapleural fibrinolytic + DNase (MIST-2 protocol) for loculated empyema
VATS or surgical decortication for failed drainage
DVT prophylaxis with LMWH unless contraindicated
stress ulcer prophylaxis in mechanically ventilated patients
glycemic control 140-180 mg/dL
early enteral nutrition within 48 hours when feasible
antipyretics (acetaminophen) for symptomatic fever; avoid in septic shock where temperature regulation is dysregulated
CURB-65 or PSI for site-of-care decision and severity stratification
daily reassessment of antibiotic appropriateness, source control adequacy, and de-escalation opportunity
smoking cessation counseling at every encounter
pneumococcal vaccination (PCV15/20 ± PPSV23) and annual influenza vaccination administered before discharge for unvaccinated patients
early mobilization and pulmonary rehabilitation referral for elderly with persistent functional decline
follow-up CXR at 6-8 weeks in patients >50 or smokers to confirm resolution and exclude underlying malignancy
counseling on biphasic illness pattern: any worsening after initial improvement (especially fever, dyspnea, pleuritic pain) warrants immediate re-evaluation
